scenario: AITA for telling someone disabled they should leave the gym | Throwaway for the usual reasons I go to the gym a few times a week as it's something I enjoy. Yesterday I was there for the first time this year and there was lots of new people which is to be expected this time of year with people making resolutions they can't stick to. Anyway I was minding my own business when I looked up and saw an overweight woman come in who had a walking stick, she also had who turned out to be her husband with her who looked like a gym regular. I saw her get on the exercise bike for about 20 minutes then she moved to the weight machines. Because of her disability she couldn't manage on and off the machines herself and her husband was helping her on and off between his workout. I was concerned about this and no staff were about so I went upto her and told her I think it's for the best she leaves the gym as she's clearly not able bodied enough for it (looking back now I should have worded it better). Her husband then came up and asked if everything was ok and I told him my concerns. He raised his voice slightly at me and told me to mind my own business as he's qualified in training different sports and she was in safe hands. I then told them I don't think the gym management would be too happy at someone disabled and unable to get on and off the machines being in the gym. He told me his wife wasn't actually allowed to join the gym without a Dr's letter and also a meeting with the gym manager to come up with a plan for her to safety evacuate the building with the help of staff and all staff were aware of her problems. At this point I realised they weren't going to leave so went back to my workout. Today I told my friend what happened and he told me I'm an idiot who should learn to mind his own business or try encourage someone who's new to the gym. He doesn't attend the gym so I don't feel he understands the kind of environment she was in. He also seems to think my membership could be at risk for what I said

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario did the right thing by telling the disabled woman to leave the gym. Let me break this down step by step. First, the person went to the gym a few times a week and noticed a lot of new people, which is common around New Year's. They saw an overweight woman with a walking stick and her husband, who seemed like a regular. The woman used the exercise bike and then moved to the weight machines, needing her husband's help to get on and off. The person was concerned because there were no staff around, so they approached her and suggested she leave, saying she wasn't able-bodied enough. Her husband got upset, explained he's qualified in training, and mentioned she had a doctor's note and a plan with the gym manager for emergencies. The person then realized they weren't going to leave and went back to their workout. Later, their friend told them they were an idiot and should mind their own business. So, the question is: was it right or wrong for the person to tell the woman to leave the gym? I think about the person's intentions. They were concerned for the woman's safety because she needed help and there were no staff around. But the way they approached her was probably not the best. Telling someone to leave because they're disabled might come off as insensitive or even discriminatory. The husband's reaction shows that the woman had proper clearance and a safety plan, so the person's concern might have been unnecessary. The gym staff were aware of her situation, which means they had measures in place to handle her needs safely. Also, the person's friend pointed out that they should encourage rather than discourage. Gyms are places for everyone, including those with disabilities, to work out. Encouraging someone, especially a new member, is more supportive than telling them to leave. Another angle is the legal aspect. In many places, discrimination against people with disabilities is illegal, and suggesting someone leave because of their disability could be seen as discriminatory. So, putting it all together, the person's intention was to help, but their approach was wrong. They should have handled the situation more sensitively, perhaps by informing the staff instead of confronting the woman directly. Encouraging and supporting, rather than discouraging, is the better approach.
